title: Uniform acceleration equations (SUVAT)
summary: Five equations link displacement, initial velocity, final velocity, constant acceleration, and time. Learn to pick the right one by spotting the missing variable.

u.label: $u$
u.meaning: initial velocity at the start of the time interval, in m/s
u.body: The velocity when your stopwatch starts ($t = 0$). It carries a sign to show direction along the line.
u.example: A car cruising at $20\text{ m/s}$ right before braking has $u = +20\text{ m/s}$.
u.analogy: The speedometer reading the instant you press start on a stopwatch.

v.label: $v$
v.meaning: final velocity at the end of the time interval, in m/s
v.body: The velocity at time $t$. Phrases like *comes to a complete stop* hide the number $v = 0\text{ m/s}$.
v.example: A braking car that stops completely has $v = 0\text{ m/s}$.
v.analogy: The speedometer reading when you hit stop on the stopwatch.

a.label: $a$
a.meaning: constant acceleration along the line, in m/s²
a.body: How much velocity changes every second. When it has the **opposite sign** to the velocity, it slows the object down (for example, $a < 0$ when moving in the positive direction).
a.example: Braking at $a = -4\text{ m/s}^2$ removes $4\text{ m/s}$ of speed every second.
a.analogy: A steady hand turning the speedometer needle up or down at a fixed rate.

t.label: $t$
t.meaning: time elapsed during the constant-acceleration motion, in seconds
t.body: Always positive. When the problem never mentions time, the timeless equation $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ lets you bypass it.
t.example: Dropping from $20\text{ m/s}$ to $0$ at $-4\text{ m/s}^2$ takes $t = 5\text{ s}$.
t.analogy: How many seconds pass on the stopwatch between start and stop.

s.label: $s$
s.meaning: displacement from the starting position, in meters
s.body: Directed straight-line change in position. Equal to distance travelled only when the object does not reverse direction.
s.example: Braking from $20\text{ m/s}$ to rest at $-4\text{ m/s}^2$ covers $s = 50\text{ m}$.
s.analogy: The distance painted on the road between the brake line and the stop line.

const_a.label: constant $a$
const_a.meaning: acceleration stays fixed in both magnitude and direction
const_a.body: The gatekeeper condition for all five {suvat|SUVAT equations}. If acceleration changes, split the motion into segments where it is constant.
const_a.example: Steady braking on dry asphalt has nearly constant $a$; hitting a bumpy patch changes it.
const_a.analogy: A straight-line slope on a $v\text{–}t$ graph.

missing_var.title: Pick by the missing variable
missing_var.body: Every {suvat|SUVAT equation} connects **four** of the five variables ([s:$s$], [u:$u$], [v:$v$], [a:$a$], [t:$t$]) and leaves out **one**. List the three you know and the one you want — whichever fifth variable is neither known nor wanted names the exact formula to use.
missing_var.useWhen: you have listed your givens and goal and are unsure which of the five equations to write down.
missing_var.example: Know $u, v, a$ and want $s$? Time $t$ is missing, so pick $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.

sign_rule.title: Sign convention in 1D
sign_rule.body: Because [s:displacement], {speed_vel|velocity}, and {acceleration|acceleration} are vectors, choose **one** direction along the line as positive (usually the initial direction of motion). Any vector pointing the opposite way gets a minus sign.
sign_rule.useWhen: an object slows down, brakes, or reverses direction.
sign_rule.example: Moving right at $20\text{ m/s}$ while braking: $u = +20\text{ m/s}$, $a = -4\text{ m/s}^2$.

sections.title: Five variables, five equations
sections.body:
Whenever an object moves along a straight line with [const_a:constant acceleration], just two ideas — the definition of {acceleration|acceleration} ($v = u + at$) and the {mean_speed|mean speed theorem} ($s = \frac{u+v}{2}t$) — generate the entire set of five {suvat|uniform acceleration equations}.

Each equation links four of the five quantities ([s:$s$], [u:$u$], [v:$v$], [a:$a$], [t:$t$]) and omits one. You never need to guess: use {missing_var|the missing-variable rule}, and keep signs consistent with {sign_rule|one positive direction}.

sections.title: Worked problem
sections.body:
A car travels along a straight road at [u:$u = 20\text{ m/s}$]. The driver spots a red light and brakes with a [const_a:constant acceleration] of [a:$a = -4\text{ m/s}^2$] until the car [v:comes to a complete stop].

Find (1) the stopping [s:displacement $s$], and (2) the [t:stopping time $t$].

sections.title: Read the givens
sections.note: take the forward direction as positive; notice the hidden zero

rows.note: negative because braking opposes forward motion ({sign_rule|sign rule})
hidden in the words *comes to a complete stop*
we know 3 variables ($u, v, a$), so any fourth can be found directly

sections.title: Plan
sections.note: choose the equation that matches what you already know

routes.title: Route A: find $s$ without $t$, then find $t$
routes.why: We know [u:$u$], [v:$v$], and [a:$a$]. By {missing_var|the missing-variable rule}, omitting [t:$t$] gives [s:$s$] in one step, and omitting [s:$s$] gives [t:$t$] in one step.
routes.whyNot: Nothing — both steps use only the original givens, so a slip in one does not corrupt the other.

routes.title: Route B: start straight with $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$
routes.why: It is the most familiar displacement formula.
routes.whyNot: It contains **two** unknowns ([s:$s$] and [t:$t$]) at once, so you cannot solve it until you find [t:$t$] first.

routes.title: Route C: use $s = ut$
routes.whyNot: Using {avg_speed|constant-speed} $s = ut$ ignores braking; the car slows from $20\text{ m/s}$ down to $0$, so its average speed is half as large.

sections.notUsed: Not used: mass or braking force. Kinematics describes motion from $u, v, a, s, t$ alone without needing Newton's laws.

sections.title: Work it through
sections.note: hover a step to see which parts it uses and what mistake to avoid

steps.move: Find the stopping [s:displacement] with the equation that omits [t:time].
steps.why: We know [u:$u = 20$], [v:$v = 0$], and [a:$a = -4$], while [t:$t$] is unknown, so {suvat|$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$} solves directly for [s:$s$].
steps.whyNot: Do not plug $+4$ for [a:$a$]: that would give $s = -50\text{ m}$ behind the car, because a car speeding forward cannot stop under positive acceleration.

steps.move: Find the [t:stopping time] from the definition of {acceleration|acceleration}.
steps.why: Losing $4\text{ m/s}$ every second from $20\text{ m/s}$ takes exactly $20/4 = 5\text{ s}$.
steps.whyNot: Do not swap [u:$u$] and [v:$v$]: setting $20 = 0 + (-4)t$ would give a negative time $t = -5\text{ s}$.

steps.move: Cross-check [s:$s$] with the quadratic formula $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$.
steps.why: Both equations come from the same [const_a:constant acceleration] model, so they must agree.
steps.whyNot: Do not drop the $\frac{1}{2}$ factor: $20(5) - 4(25) = 0\text{ m}$, which is impossible while moving forward.

steps.why: Because acceleration is constant, the average velocity over the $5\text{ s}$ is halfway between $20$ and $0$, which is $10\text{ m/s}$.
steps.whyNot: This averaging shortcut works **only** for [const_a:constant acceleration], never when $a$ varies.

sections.title: See how acceleration bends displacement
sections.note: starts at the braking problem (u = 20, a = -4, t = 5); drag u, a, and t to explore

sections.title: Check yourself
items: **Condition**: all five {suvat|SUVAT equations} require [const_a:constant acceleration]; never apply them across a sudden change in $a$.
**Signs**: slowing down does **not** always mean $a < 0$ — it means [a:$a$] and velocity have **opposite signs** ({sign_rule|sign rule}).
**Hidden zeros**: *starts from rest* means [u:$u = 0$]; *comes to a stop* means [v:$v = 0$].
**Units**: convert $\text{km/h}$ to $\text{m/s}$ (divide by $3.6$) before substituting into any formula.
**Size check**: for braking to rest, $s = \frac{1}{2}ut$ is exactly half the distance the car would travel at constant [u:$u$], as the plot shows ($50\text{ m}$ vs $100\text{ m}$).

sections.title: Recall
sections.note: work each answer in your head before revealing

questions.q: A scooter accelerates uniformly from $u = 4\text{ m/s}$ at $a = 2\text{ m/s}^2$ for $t = 3\text{ s}$. What is its displacement $s$?
questions.why: $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2 = 4(3) + \frac{1}{2}(2)(3^2) = 12 + 9 = 21\text{ m}$. Dropping $\frac{1}{2}$ gives $30\text{ m}$, and ignoring $a$ gives $12\text{ m}$.

questions.q: A problem gives $u$, $v$, and $s$, and asks for constant acceleration $a$ (time $t$ is never mentioned). Which equation solves it in one step?
questions.why: By {missing_var|the missing-variable rule}, since $t$ is neither given nor wanted, choose the timeless equation $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.

questions.q: A car slows uniformly from $12\text{ m/s}$ to rest over $18\text{ m}$. What is its acceleration $a$?
questions.why: Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$: $0^2 = 12^2 + 2a(18) \implies 36a = -144 \implies a = -4\text{ m/s}^2$. Forgetting the factor of $2$ gives $-8\text{ m/s}^2$.

questions.q: Why does $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$ give the wrong displacement when an object starts with $u = 10\text{ m/s}$?
options: Because it omits the initial-velocity term $ut$
questions.why: The full formula is $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$. Both $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$ and $v^2 = 2as$ are shortcuts that hold only when $u = 0$.
